o: Describe how linear search checks each item in turn.
Trace a small search using indices.
Recognise that the list does not need sorting.
r: Identify the flowchart shape used for a decision.
Write a Boolean condition to check if x is greater than 10.
Trace: x = 4; if x > 3 then x = x + 5 endif; print(x).
c: A sequential scan
Linear search starts at one end of a collection and compares one element at a time with the target.
Zero-based indices
The first array element is at index 0, then 1, 2, etc. Do not confuse index with value.
Stopping
If the target is found, report its index. If the list ends without a match, report not found.
One strength
Linear search works even if values are unsorted, though it may need to inspect the entire list.

m.q: Trace linear search for 8 in [3, 9, 1, 8, 5]. Give the comparisons and index.
st: Start at index 0 and compare 3 with 8: no match.
Index 1: 9 is not 8.
Index 2: 1 is not 8.
Index 3: 8 matches the target.
Report found at index 3 after four comparisons.

w: Search [7, 2, 6, 4] for 6. Which elements are compared?
7, 2, then 6. Found at index 2 after three comparisons.
Search [7, 2, 6, 4] for 9. What should be returned?
Not found, after checking all four elements.
Must this array be sorted for linear search? Explain.
No. Linear search works with unsorted values because it checks sequentially.

k.q: Predict the index printed by this short linear-search program.
k.code:
array values = [5,3,8]
for i = 0 to 2
    if values[i] == 8 then
        print(i)
    endif
next i
p: Explain why this program does not print anything if the target is absent.
k.a: Searching for 8 prints index 2; searching for 3 prints index 1. If no value matches, no print statement runs. A complete search program should explicitly report not found.

e: State one requirement for linear search to work on a list. [1 mark]
It can work with unsorted data [1]; no sorting is required.
Search [9, 4, 1, 6] for 1. State each comparison and the zero-based index returned. [3 marks]
Compare 9 [1], 4 [1], then 1 at index 2 [1].
Explain how linear search would find 7 in an unsorted list [3, 8, 7, 1], or report failure. [4 marks]
Start at first element [1]; compare sequentially 3, 8, 7 [1]; report index 2 when found [1]; if end reached with no match report not found [1].
v: Checks items one by one for a target.
Position used to access an array item, starting at zero.
Checking an item against a value or condition.
x: Linear search can only work when a list is already sorted.

o: Explain how bubble sort compares neighbouring values.
Describe insertion sort's growing sorted section.
r: Checking values in turn until target is found or the list ends.
Where is index 0 in a one-dimensional array?
Does linear search require sorted data?
A list is [4, 2, 9, 1]. How many comparisons are made to find 9 with linear search?
c: Bubble sort
Compare adjacent values and swap those in the wrong order; repeat passes until no swaps are needed.
After each pass
For ascending bubble sort, the largest remaining value moves towards the end on each full pass.
Insertion sort
Treat the first item as a sorted section; take the next key item and insert it into the correct place.
Keep a trace
Show each swap or insertion rather than jumping straight to the final sorted result.

m.q: Show one full bubble-sort pass through [5, 1, 4, 2].
st: Compare 5 and 1: swap → [1, 5, 4, 2].
Compare 5 and 4: swap → [1, 4, 5, 2].
Compare 5 and 2: swap → [1, 4, 2, 5].
End of first pass: 5 has reached its final position.
More passes are needed to sort the remaining values.

w: Perform one bubble-sort pass on [4, 2, 3].
For insertion sort on [6, 2, 5], show what happens when inserting 2 into the sorted section.
Begin [6]; insert 2 before 6 → [2, 6, 5].
Finish insertion sort on [2, 6, 5].
Insert 5 between 2 and 6 → [2, 5, 6].

k.q: Predict the output after one adjacent comparison and swap.
k.code:
a = 5
b = 2
if a > b then
    temp = a
    a = b
    b = temp
endif
print(a)
p: Change the first value of a to 1.
Explain how comparing neighbouring values is used in bubble sort.
k.a: Initially 2 is printed because 5 and 2 swap. If a = 1 and b = 2, no swap takes place, so 1 prints. Bubble sort uses such adjacent comparisons repeatedly.

e: State what bubble sort compares. [1 mark]
Adjacent (neighbouring) values [1].
Show one bubble-sort pass on [3, 1, 2], giving the array after each swap. [3 marks]
[1, 3, 2] [1]; [1, 2, 3] [1]; largest item reaches end [1].
Explain how insertion sort orders the list [4, 1, 3]. [4 marks]
First item 4 is initial sorted section [1]; insert 1 before 4 → [1, 4, 3] [1]; take key 3 [1]; insert between 1 and 4 → [1, 3, 4] [1].
v: Repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent out-of-order values.
Inserts each next item into a growing sorted section.
One traversal of adjacent values in a sort.
Current value being inserted into a sorted section.
x: One bubble-sort pass always completely sorts any list.

016.t: Variables, Input, Output and One-Dimensional Arrays
o: Assign and update variables using OCR ERL.
Identify input and output in short programs.
Use zero-based indexes in one-dimensional arrays.
r: What is the first array index in OCR ERL?
c: Variables
A variable stores a value that can be updated using assignment. Use meaningful names.
Input and output
Input obtains information from a user or device; output displays or sends information.
Arrays
A one-dimensional array stores related values under one name, accessed using indexes.
Zero-based indexing
Index 0 is the first value; index 1 is the second, so the index differs from counting positions in everyday speech.

m.q: Trace the array and variable assignments in a short quiz-mark program.
st: Create marks = [4, 7, 9]. The first value has index 0.
Set total = marks[0] + marks[1], giving 11.
Update marks[0] to 5.
Recalculate total = marks[0] + marks[1] to obtain 12.
Output total; explain why the value changed.

w: Write an assignment that stores 12 in a variable called score.
score = 12.
For array marks = [6, 3, 8], identify marks[1].
Update marks[0] to 10 and calculate marks[0] + marks[2].

k.q: Predict the output of an array access and a variable update.
k.code:
array marks = [6,3,8]
score = marks[0]
score = score + marks[1]
print(score)
p: Write one assignment to store the last array element in score.
k.a: 6 + 3 = 9. After changing the middle element to 5, output = 11. To retrieve last item, score = marks[2].

e: State one difference between a variable and an array. [2 marks]
Variable can store a value [1]; array contains an indexed collection of values [1].
Given values = [7, 2, 5], state the values at indices 0 and 2. [2 marks]
Index 0 is 7 [1]; index 2 is 5 [1].
Write OCR ERL assignments to set total to 0, add values[0] and values[1], then display total. [4 marks]
total = 0 [1]; total = total + values[0] [1]; total = total + values[1] [1]; print(total) [1].
v: Named storage for a value in a program.
Storing or updating a variable's value.
Indexed collection of values stored under one name.
Number specifying an array element's position.
x: The element at index 2 is normally the third element of an OCR ERL array.

o: Explain defensive design and input validation.
Select normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous test data.
r: Named storage for a program value.
Give the first index of an array.
State what output means in a program.
For array [4, 8, 2], update index 1 to 5 and state the sum of indices 0 and 1.
c: Robust programs
Defensive design anticipates invalid or malicious input and uses readable, maintainable code.
Validation
Validation checks input against rules such as type, length or range. It does not verify a person's identity.
Authentication
Authentication establishes identity, for example using credentials or another factor.
Testing
Use normal, boundary, invalid and erroneous values; compare expected and actual results. Test during development and again at the end.

m.q: A program accepts a mark from 0 to 100 inclusive. Choose test data and explain the expected results.
st: Write the validation rule: 0 <= mark <= 100.
Choose normal data: 56 → accepted.
Choose boundary data: 0 and 100 → accepted.
Choose invalid data of the correct type: -1 or 101 → rejected.
Choose erroneous data of the wrong type, e.g. 'hello' → rejected or handled safely.

w: Classify input 50 for a 0–100 mark rule and state expected outcome.
Normal valid data; accepted.
Classify 100 and 101.
100 is valid upper boundary and accepted; 101 is invalid and rejected.
Why can a valid username format fail authentication?
Validation checks format; authentication checks identity/credentials and can still fail.

k.q: Predict the result of a range validation check.
k.code:
mark = 101
if mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100 then
    print("Accepted")
else
    print("Rejected")
endif
p: Give one erroneous (wrong-type) value and explain why numeric comparison needs suitable input handling.
k.a: 101 prints Rejected; 100 prints Accepted. An erroneous value such as 'hello' has the wrong type and should be rejected before numerical comparison to avoid an error.

e: Define input validation. [2 marks]
Checking input against specified rules [1], rejecting unsuitable data before processing [1].
Give two boundary values and one invalid value for marks from 0 to 100 inclusive. [3 marks]
Boundary 0 [1] and 100 [1]; invalid e.g. 101 or -1 [1].
Distinguish authentication and validation; explain why iterative testing is useful. [4 marks]
Authentication checks identity [1]; validation checks data against rules [1]; iterative testing happens during development [1], identifying and correcting faults early [1].
v: Designing programs to handle invalid input and misuse.
Checking entered data against defined rules.
Valid data at the extreme limits of an allowed range.
x: Validation and authentication mean exactly the same thing.

w: A 5 × 4 bitmap at 8 bits per pixel uses how many bytes?
5 × 4 × 8 = 160 bits = 20 bytes.
Linear search for 6 in [2, 5, 6, 1]: give the zero-based index.
Index 2.
State what the PC holds and why the FDE cycle repeats.
PC holds next instruction address; repeated cycles process successive instructions.

k.q: Predict the raw number of bits in a bitmap.
k.code:
width = 10
height = 5
depth = 8
print(width * height * depth)
p: Explain how to convert the result to bytes.
k.a: 10 × 5 × 8 = 400 bits. At 4-bit depth, 200 bits. Divide bits by 8: 25 bytes at 4-bit depth. Code is a small retrieval task, not a substitute for the assessment.
